name: Nair depilatory

card.summary: Classic drugstore depilatory cream: dissolves hair at the surface, regrows in days, irritation is the main caveat.
card.note: Alkaline chemistry; labels advise patch testing.

lead: Nair is an American brand of chemical depilatory creams, lotions and sprays that people use to remove unwanted body and facial hair without a razor. The product is spread on, left for a few minutes, then wiped or rinsed off, leaving the skin smooth. [1][2]

Wikipedia reports that the original Nair lotion launched in 1940, that the name blends "no hair", and that Church & Dwight makes it after Carter-Wallace sold the brand in 2001. [1] A men's line launched in 2001, and by 2007 the brand sold 25 products including waxes and bleaches. [1] Its advertising included a television spot with the line "We wear short shorts, Nair for short shorts," which won a Clio and echoed a 1958 song. [1]

Nair depilatories contain calcium hydroxide and, in some formulas, potassium thioglycolate, which attack the disulfide bonds in hair keratin so the hair breaks down and can be wiped away. Softening agents such as mineral oil are included to offset the harsh active ingredients. [1] Depilatories work above the skin surface and do not reach the dermal papilla, so hair regrows. [2] Grokipedia also covers the brand. [3] No clinical studies specific to the brand were found.

chain: Alkaline cream dissolves keratin in the hair shaft
Hair is wiped away at the skin surface in about ten minutes
angle.text: Depilatory creams remove hair at skin level from larger areas such as legs, arms, chest or upper lip with no razor, and users value the smooth finish. Because the root is untouched, hair grows back, so the result lasts for a short period.

infobox: Calcium hydroxide; potassium thioglycolate in some formulas [1]

paras: The original Nair lotion launched in 1940. A television campaign built on the 1958 song "Short Shorts" won a Clio Award, a men's line was added in 2001, and by 2007 the brand sold about 25 products including waxes and bleaches. [1]

Depilatories in general have a long history: Wikipedia notes that Greek and Roman writers described depilatory ointments and plasters, that older products used sulfides such as strontium sulfide until their odor led manufacturers to switch to thiols, and that depilatories are sold today in gel, cream, lotion, aerosol, roll-on and powder forms. [2]

Thiol salts, mainly calcium thioglycolate at about 5 to 6 percent in a cream base, break disulfide bonds in keratin so the hair weakens and wipes off, while a hydroxide such as calcium hydroxide holds the pH near 12. Hair breakdown takes about ten minutes, after which the skin is rinsed with water and conditioner may be applied. [2]
Wikipedia notes that depilatories are also used medically for hirsutism associated with polycystic ovary syndrome. [2]

Wikipedia notes only that the active ingredients are harsh, which is why softening agents are included. [1] Product labels commonly advise patch testing and limits on application time; these are manufacturer instructions. No clinical safety data specific to Nair were found.

timeline.event: The song "Short Shorts" is released; a later Nair ad built on it wins a Clio. [1]
Carter-Wallace sells the brand to Church & Dwight; a men's line launches. [1]

quick.overview:
Nair is a long-running chemical hair remover, launched in 1940 and now owned by Church & Dwight. It is sold in women's and men's lines.

It is a temporary method: the follicle is left intact so hair grows back.
quick.mechanism: Thioglycolate or calcium hydroxide breaks keratin's disulfide bonds so the hair can be wiped off.
quick.risks: Harsh actives can irritate skin; no brand-specific clinical studies were found.
